opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I learned the hard way, honestly. Back when I was at Google and then at DeepMind, we did the data center cooling work, using reinforcement learning to optimize the cooling systems. The results were remarkable. We were seeing something like 30 to 40 percent energy savings on cooling in some of those facilities. And everybody got very excited, and rightfully so.

But what struck me over time was the gap between a great result and real-world impact at scale. A research breakthrough proves something is possible. It doesn't mean that thing is running in thousands of facilities around the world, saving energy every single day. To get from one to the other, you have to solve a whole set of problems that have nothing to do with the core algorithm. How do you integrate with the control systems that are already there, some of which are decades old? How do you earn the trust of the operators, the people who've been running these plants for twenty or thirty years and who are ultimately responsible if something goes wrong? How do you handle safety, explainability, and edge cases? How do you deploy it repeatably, without a team of PhDs flying out to every site?

That's what productization really is. It's taking something that works brilliantly in one carefully managed setting and making it work reliably, safely, and cheaply everywhere else. And the uncomfortable truth is that's usually the harder part. The model might be 20 percent of the effort and everything around it is the other 80.

So for me, if you care about impact, whether that's reducing energy consumption or cutting emissions in industrial facilities, you can't stop at the paper or the pilot. The impact only happens when the technology is actually in people's hands, running in production, day after day. That conviction is a big part of why we started Phaidra. We wanted to take what we'd seen was possible and build it into something industrial operators could actually adopt and depend on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says impact happens when technology is in people’s hands and running in production day after day.

r002.rationale: The candidate says productization is usually harder, estimating the model at 20% of the effort and everything around it at 80%.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, this comes from a pretty painful lesson I learned at DeepMind. We did the data center cooling project with Google, and it worked. We cut cooling energy by something like 40 percent, there was a blog post, people were excited. And then I remember sitting there a few months later realizing that the research result was the easy part. The hard part was everything after that.

Because what we had built was basically a demo. It ran in one facility, with a team of PhDs babysitting it, with a custom integration into that specific building's control system. And the question that kept nagging me was, okay, this is great, but what about the other thousands of buildings in the world that have cooling plants? None of them have a DeepMind team on call. None of them are going to let you spend a year on a bespoke integration.

So that's really where the conviction comes from. If you want a technology to change the world, it has to be able to walk into a building on its own and work. It has to be robust to messy data, to sensors that fail, to operators who don't trust it yet. It has to be safe enough that a facilities manager who has been doing this for 30 years is willing to hand over the controls. And it has to be economically viable, meaning the cost of deploying it has to be a small fraction of the value it creates, otherwise it just doesn't scale.

None of that is research in the traditional sense. It's product work. It's unglamorous, it's a lot of plumbing, it's a lot of listening to customers tell you why your beautiful algorithm doesn't matter to them. But I've come to believe that's actually where most of the impact gets created or lost. You can have the best model in the world, and if it only exists in a paper or a one-off pilot, the carbon is still going into the atmosphere.

That's a big reason I started Phaidra. The thesis was essentially: the AI is ready, the gap is productization. Let's close that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says AI must work in ordinary buildings and be trusted by facilities managers to change the world, making real-world adoption necessary for impact.

r002.rationale: It calls the research result the easy part and says the hard work comes afterward, describing extensive integration, reliability, safety, and customer-facing product work.

astra-6.text:
Because the technology itself is only a starting point. You can build a really impressive model, but until it’s helping somebody solve a real problem, you haven’t actually created impact. A product is what connects that capability to something people can use and rely on.

And that forces you to answer questions that a technical demonstration can leave open: Does this fit into someone’s workflow? Is it reliable? Is the benefit worth the effort of adopting it? Those aren’t peripheral questions. They determine whether the technology makes a difference.

So I see product development as part of realizing the potential of AI. You have to close that loop between what the technology can do and what people actually need.

r001.rationale: The response says AI creates impact when it helps people solve real problems and is something they can use and rely on.

r002.rationale: It says product development connects AI capabilities to people's needs, but does not state that it requires vastly more work than developing the technology itself.

sol-6.1.text: Because the technology itself is only the starting point. You can have an incredibly capable model, but if it never gets integrated into how people actually work, it doesn’t change anything. Turning it into a product means understanding a real problem, making the system reliable and easy to use, and delivering a result that somebody cares about. That’s where you close the loop between what AI can do in principle and the value it creates in practice.
